title: Astaghfirullah, a hundred times
hook: asking forgiveness a hundred times a day, as he did (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday: tahlil, la ilaha illallah, the card that outweighs the scrolls. Your line was there is only one. Today, a word said a hundred times a day.

How many times did you say sorry yesterday? Maybe a dozen. Sorry, bumped your cart. Sorry, running late. Sorry, can you say that again? Most of those aren't really apologies; they're grease on the gears of the day. How many times did you really ask to be forgiven? Maybe once. Maybe not at all. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ tells the people: O people, turn to Allah in repentance, for I turn to Him a hundred times a day. A hundred.
screen: `A DOZEN SORRYS A DAY.` → `HOW MANY REAL ONES?` → `A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: The word is astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness. Saying it is called istighfar. The root, gh-f-r, means to cover, to shield; Arabic dictionaries list a soldier's helmet, mighfar, from the same root. So forgiveness, in this picture, isn't just wiping a slate. It's being covered, protected from what the mistake would otherwise do. Now the surprise. Muslims generally hold that the Prophet was protected from serious sin, though the schools describe that protection differently. So why ask forgiveness a hundred times a day? Scholars give a few answers. Some say humility: the closer a person is to God, the more they notice the distance. Some say teaching: he did it so his community would. A version of the hadith says: something covers my heart, a kind of cloud, and I ask forgiveness a hundred times a day. In Bukhari, the number is more than seventy. And it's not only about sins. Istighfar is said three times at the end of the prayer, right after the taslim, as if to say: I tried, and it wasn't perfect. The Qur'an adds a promise. In Surah Nuh, the prophet Nuh tells his people: ask forgiveness of your Lord, and He will send rain, and help you with wealth and sons, and give you gardens and rivers. Asking forgiveness, paired with rain. There's also a longer form, the master of all istighfar, reported in Bukhari. But the short one, one word, is the one people carry all day.
screen: `GH-F-R — TO COVER, TO SHIELD.` · `WHY WOULD HE NEED IT?` · `THREE TIMES, AFTER THE PRAYER.` · `ASK, AND THE RAIN COMES.` · then, large: `A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Rest your right hand, palm up. If you pray, say astaghfirullah on each finger joint, not rushing, and let a face or a moment come to mind now and then, something you'd like covered; if you don't, say sorry silently on each count, and mean some of them. Go slowly; you won't reach a hundred, and that's fine.
Istighfar. Saying astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness; to be covered and shielded, a hundred times a day. Today's word.
Your line: I ask forgiveness. One word, and a cover. That's day one hundred eighteen.

screen: `DAY 118 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PRAYERS ON THE PROPHET ﷺ.`

howItsDone: Muslims say astaghfirullah three times right after finishing each prayer, and many repeat it through the day, sometimes a hundred times, following the Prophet's example.

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm.

'Muslims believe the Prophet was protected from serious sin' ('isma): Sunni and Shia positions differ in scope (Shia hold complete infallibility). Now worded as 'Muslims generally hold... though the schools describe that protection differently'; a Keeper may want to refine.
The explanations for the Prophet's istighfar (humility, teaching, the ghain on the heart) are among several scholarly views.
